reason: E3 directly supports the premise that laser cladding provides controlled heat input for repairing Cr-Ni-Mo steels prone to hot cracking. E1 and E2 support that HEAs can be deposited by laser cladding and improve surface properties, but they do not provide specific evidence for the claimed refined microstructure, metallurgical bonding, or the 20-40% hardness increase, nor do they address hot cracking reduction in the specific substrate.
premises: Laser cladding provides confined, controlled heat input, reducing thermal stresses and hot cracking risk compared to fusion welding.
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can be deposited by laser cladding for surface modification.
HEA coatings can improve hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance.
Rapid solidification in laser cladding produces a refined, metallurgically bonded microstructure.
The substrate material (e.g., 34CrNiMo6) is susceptible to hot cracking during high heat input repair.
